examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
examples.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={z}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2z\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=z\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{{z}^{2}}\cdot z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{z}^{2}}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
